title: Disappearing Messages and Stolen Phones: Unanswered Questions in the Mandelson Affair
summary: The release of over 1,500 pages of documents on Lord Peter Mandelson's appointment as UK ambassador to the US has left more questions than answers. MPs had demanded transparency after Mandelson was sacked amid scrutiny over his role and his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. But crucial gaps remain. First, Prime Minister Keir Starmer uses disappearing messages on his phone. Downing Street confirmed this, saying it's permitted as long as it doesn't impact record-keeping. Yet only six messages between Starmer and Mandelson appear in the files, leaving critics to wonder what was lost. Second, two key officials had their phones stolen. Morgan McSweeney, Starmer's former chief of staff who championed Mandelson's appointment, reported his government phone stolen last year; police haven't recovered it. Cabinet Office Minister Nick Thomas-Symonds also had his personal phone stolen, which he says contained messages with Mandelson. Third, Mandelson's vetting form—a nine-page summary of security clearance—is missing from the released documents. A blank template was published, but not his completed form or his declaration of interests. Finally, answers to three follow-up questions McSweeney asked Mandelson about his Epstein ties are being withheld at the request of the Metropolitan Police, who are investigating Mandelson for misconduct in public office. Mandelson denies wrongdoing. The redactions and missing material leave the full story frustratingly out of reach.
why_it_matters: This affair tests whether transparency rules designed to hold powerful officials accountable can keep up with modern communication tools like auto-deleting messages, and raises uncomfortable questions about who gets a pass in the vetting process — issues that affect all citizens’ trust in government.

background_read: Lord Peter Mandelson (a senior British politician and former Labour cabinet minister, one of the architects of the party’s modernisation under Tony Blair) was given the high-profile post of ambassador to Washington, a role usually reserved for career diplomats or trusted allies.

Jeffrey Epstein (the American financier convicted of sex trafficking who died in 2019) had a wide network of powerful contacts, and any association with him has become politically toxic, raising questions about influence and judgment.

Downing Street (the official residence and office of the UK Prime Minister) has strict rules on record-keeping for transparency, but the use of disappearing messages has sparked criticism that it could undermine the public’s right to know.

Security vetting for top posts normally includes a detailed declaration of interests and rigorous background checks by the Cabinet Office; the absence of Mandelson’s completed form is unusual and adds to suspicions.

The Metropolitan Police (often called the Met, the police force for Greater London) is investigating possible misconduct, which legally allows them to request that certain evidence be kept from the public during an active inquiry.

perspectives.description: MPs and transparency campaigners argue that the release of over 1,500 pages, even with gaps, shows the system can work under pressure. They see the public spotting of missing items — like the vetting form — as proof that outside scrutiny is essential and may force further disclosures.

Critics say the gaps are too convenient: disappearing messages, stolen phones, and withheld answers create a wall behind which misconduct can hide. They fear that if senior officials can lawfully avoid creating records, the government effectively operates without real oversight.

From a procedural standpoint, it is not unusual for police investigations to limit what can be released, and the use of disappearing messages has been allowed for certain government business. The real tension is between a legitimate active police inquiry and the public’s expectation of transparency in a high-profile appointment.

The ongoing Met investigation could lead to charges or clear Mandelson, but either outcome will spark debate on whether the rules on official communications need tightening — for example, banning disappearing apps for government business. Future appointments may face stricter vetting to avoid a repeat of this saga.
